title: I have, I don't have
goal: Master possession completely — and the machine that drives it: prepositions that take personal endings, a pattern that repeats all through Hebrew.
bekal: saying what you have and don't have
using לִי, לְךָ, לוֹ and their relatives
building sentences with אִתִּי, אֶצְלִי, בִּשְׁבִילִי

dialogs.title: שִׂיחָה — מִי לָקַח אֶת הַמַּפְתֵּחַ?
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon at the apartment. Budi can't find his keys.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: דָּנָה, יֵשׁ לָךְ אֶת הַמַּפְתֵּחַ שֶׁלִּי?
lines.baca: danah, yesh lakh et hamafte'akh sheli?
lines.id: Dana, do you have my key?

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: No, I don't. Did you check your bag?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: כֵּן. יֵשׁ לִי רַק אֶת הַטֶּלֶפוֹן וְהָאַרְנָק.
lines.baca: ken. yesh li rak et hatelefon veha'arnak.
lines.id: Yes. All I have is my phone and my wallet.
lines.literal: yes. there-is to-me only (obj) the-phone and-the-wallet.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: אֲנִי חוֹשֵׁב שֶׁלֹּא. הוּא לֹא הָיָה אִתִּי.
lines.baca: ani khoshev shelo. hu lo hayah iti.
lines.id: I don't think so. He's not with me.
lines.literal: I think that-not. he not with-me.

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: Do you have a spare key?

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.text: אָז אֵין בְּעָיָה. יֵשׁ לָךְ אֶת הַמִּסְפָּר שֶׁלָּהּ?
lines.baca: az ein be'ayah. yesh lakh et hamispar shelah?
lines.id: Then no problem. Do you have her number?
lines.literal: so there-isn't problem. there-is to-you (obj) the-number of-her (f)?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.text: יֵשׁ לִי, אֲבָל אֵין לִי סוֹלְלָה.
lines.baca: yesh li, aval ein li solelah.
lines.id: I do, but my battery's dead.
lines.literal: there-is to-me, but there-isn't to-me battery.

lines.speaker: דָּנָה:
lines.id: That's what neighbors are for, right?

notes: ⚠️ **Hebrew has no verb "to have" at all.** For "I have a book" it says יֵשׁ לִי סֵפֶר — literally **"there is to me a book"**. Notice what the subject is: not "I" but **the book**. The owner isn't the doer; there's just a thing located near someone.

**This isn't a Hebrew quirk.** Arabic, Russian and Irish do the same, and even English has a trace of it: "the book is mine", "there's a book for me". If you think "there is to me" instead of "I have", this whole unit feels natural.

⚠️ **If the thing is definite, אֶת must appear**: יֵשׁ לִי אֶת הַמַּפְתֵּחַ (I have the key). If indefinite, no אֶת: יֵשׁ לִי מַפְתֵּחַ. The אֶת rule from unit 7 applies unchanged. Israelis themselves argue about this in formal Hebrew — but in everyday speech, אֶת is used.
**אֵין is the negative, and it's never paired with לֹא.** אֵין לִי כֶּסֶף. Saying לֹא יֵשׁ is a mistake that marks you as a beginner instantly.
**אֵצֶל** (*etsel*) = "at (someone's) place", exactly like French *chez*. אֵצֶל יוֹסִי = at Yossi's. אֲנִי אֵצֶל הָרוֹפֵא = I'm at the doctor's.
**אִתִּי** = "with me". The base word is עִם (with), but with endings it becomes אִתִּ־: אִתִּי, אִתְּךָ, אִתּוֹ, אִתָּהּ, אִתָּנוּ. An exception to memorize whole.
**קַח / קְחִי** = "take" (to m / to f). Imperatives again; unit 19 takes them apart.
**בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה** = "that's what ... is for". Dana's closing line shows how everyday Hebrew is often warmer than its literal translation.

grammars.title: Prepositions that take endings — the recurring machine
body: You've met this machine three times already: שֶׁל (unit 4), אֶת (unit 7), בִּשְׁבִיל (unit 11). Here it is in full, with the most common prepositions.
after: ⚠️ Notice that **the endings are exactly the same in all four columns**: ־ִי, ־ְךָ, ־ֵךְ, ־וֹ, ־ָהּ, ־ֵנוּ, ־ְכֶם, ־ָם. You're not memorizing four tables — you're memorizing **one set of endings** and sticking it onto any preposition. That's how Hebrew saves effort: one machine, used again and again.
English has a similar set, just shorter and separate: me, you, him, her, us, them. The difference is that Hebrew marks male and female at almost every step — even for "you".

grammars.title: יֵשׁ and אֵין in full sentences
body: These four patterns cover nearly every A1 sentence about having.
after: ⚠️ The last two rows show that **יֵשׁ changes form for other tenses**: הָיָה לִי (there was to me), יִהְיֶה לִי (there will be to me). Past and future are covered in full in units 15 and 16 — but you can memorize these two sentences whole right now, because both are very common.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **מִשְׁקָפַיִם** ends in ־ַיִם, the pair marker — like מִכְנָסַיִם and נַעֲלַיִם in unit 11. Hebrew sees glasses as a pair of lenses, just as English says "a pair of glasses".

sections.title: Sentences born from the ending machine

blocks.title: Two expressions that make you sound Israeli
items: **אֵין לִי כֹּחַ** *(ein li ko'akh)* — literally "there's no strength to me", meaning "I really can't be bothered". One of the most common expressions in Israel, and almost impossible to translate exactly.
**אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג** *(ein li musag)* — "I haven't the faintest idea", for questions you truly can't answer. More honest and warmer than אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right form of לְ.
Fill in the blanks with עִם, אֵצֶל or בִּשְׁבִיל plus the right ending.

answers: אֵין לִי כֶּסֶף. — אֵין לָנוּ זְמַן. — אֵין לָהּ מְכוֹנִית. — אֵין לָהֶם בַּיִת גָּדוֹל.
יֵשׁ לְךָ זְמַן? — אֵין לִי מְזֻמָּן. — יֵשׁ לָהּ אֶת הַמַּפְתֵּחַ. — זֶה בִּשְׁבִילְכֶם. — אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג.
wave: Empty your bag onto the table and name each item with יֵשׁ לִי .... Then name five things you DON'T have with you using אֵין לִי .... Ten sentences, three minutes.
